_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-09-26 16:58:25Z)**_

Partially—yes, the core feature exists.

- After the user confirms a generated story, it is published at `/s/{unique-slug}` ([storybook-app.tsx](/Users/sreechandt/Documents/GrowthGarage/agara/components/storybook-app.tsx:179)).
- The page is accessible without signing in and returns 404 if missing or deleted ([page.tsx](/Users/sreechandt/Documents/GrowthGarage/agara/app/s/[slug]/page.tsx:15)).
- Published stories appear under “Your stories” with a link ([storybook-app.tsx](/Users/sreechandt/Documents/GrowthGarage/agara/components/storybook-app.tsx:625)).
- Pages are unlisted and excluded from search-engine indexing.

One important gap: a webpage is created only after the user clicks **Confirm changes**, not immediately when generation finishes. Also, if publishing fails, the story is still marked ready and only a warning is shown. Therefore, the strict requirement that *every generated story must have an accessible webpage* is not fully guaranteed yet.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-09-26 17:01:16Z)**_

The best fit for this product is **AssemblyAI’s pre-recorded transcription API**, using:

- `speaker_labels: true`
- `speakers_expected: 2`
- Speaker Identification with roles `["Interviewer", "Interviewee"]`
- Only the utterances labeled `Interviewee` passed into story generation

AssemblyAI is a stronger fit than the current OpenAI transcription call because it provides both speaker diarization and role identification. Its Universal-2 model supports 99 languages, including Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam, Kannada, Marathi, Punjabi, Bengali, Urdu, and English, along with code-switching and diarization. ([AssemblyAI model documentation](https://www.assemblyai.com/docs/getting-started/models), [Speaker Identification documentation](https://www.assemblyai.com/docs/speech-understanding/speaker-identification))

The resulting flow would be:

```text
Uploaded interview
        ↓
AssemblyAI transcription + two-speaker diarization
        ↓
Interviewer / Interviewee role identification
        ↓
Keep only Interviewee utterances
        ↓
Generate the story
```

Important caveat: no single-channel diarization system is perfect—especially with interruptions, laughter, overlapping speech, or one-word responses. AssemblyAI notes that speakers need enough speech for reliable identification. The interface should therefore include a short transcript review showing only the selected interviewee passages before publishing.

An even more reliable recording design would be to capture the speakers on separate audio channels or microphones. When each speaker has a dedicated channel, separation is deterministic and more accurate than AI diarization.

OpenAI now offers `gpt-4o-transcribe-diarize`, including reference clips for known speakers, and it would require the smallest code change. However, official OpenAI documentation says that model is scheduled for removal on **February 26, 2027**, so I would not build a new long-term integration around it. ([OpenAI speech-to-text documentation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/speech-to-text), [OpenAI deprecations](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/deprecations))

My recommendation: **AssemblyAI Universal-2 + diarization + role identification**, followed by interviewee-only filtering and a human review step.

Let's add something else. Once you have taken the transcription from the story, do this. Find an object or a location from the story that stands out. And then create an image for it. These are instructions for you to create that image. Use your visual knowledge of the subject to identify its most distinctive and recognisable forms. Do not create a generic interpretation. Select only the minimum visual information needed for the subject to be immediately identifiable.

## Format and background

Use a **1:1 square composition**.

Cover the entire frame with warm off-white aged paper. Give the paper subtle fibres, natural grain, faint usage marks and a matte finish. Preserve large areas of completely unprinted paper. The whitespace is an essential part of the composition.

## Stamp placement and scale

Place a single, horizontally organised, multi-colour rubber-stamp impression in the **lower-middle** of the paper.

The complete stamped scene should occupy only approximately **30%–38% of the image height**, with generous blank space around it and especially above it.

The stamp must remain a small field-note impression. Do not enlarge it into a conventional illustration, product image, landscape painting, logo, seal or poster graphic.

Do not place the stamp inside a box, circle, border or defined frame.

## Subject interpretation

First determine what makes the requested subject visually distinctive. Extract only **three to six essential forms or relationships**.

Depending on the subject, these could include:

- One defining architectural silhouette or landmark
    
- A distinctive object shape, construction or arrangement
    
- A characteristic room layout or relationship between furniture and objects
    
- A recognisable landscape contour, shoreline, road or vegetation pattern
    
- One broken, opened, cut or partially revealed detail that helps identify an object
    
- One or two secondary forms that provide context and scale
    

Preserve the subject’s defining proportions, structure and spatial relationships. Simplify aggressively without making it generic.

For a **place**, prioritise one unmistakable landmark and a restrained suggestion of its surrounding geography.

For an **object or food item**, prioritise its characteristic silhouette, construction, segmentation, layers or packaging cue.

For an **interior or remembered scene**, retain only the main spatial anchors and the objects that carry the story.

Do not assemble a catalogue of landmarks or objects. Do not reproduce every possible detail associated with the subject.

Remove people, crowds, vehicles, repetitive buildings, dense windows, excessive vegetation, decorative objects, background clutter and anything that does not contribute directly to recognition.

## Colour

Extract or select **two to four desaturated spot inks** appropriate to the subject.

Possible colours include carbon black, cocoa brown, deep green, brick red, ochre yellow, slate blue and taupe. Do not apply a predetermined palette if different colours are essential to recognising the subject.

Use:

- One dark ink for the primary contours
    
- One distinctive colour associated with the subject
    
- Up to two restrained secondary colours for context or emphasis
    

Allow the aged paper to form most highlights, empty areas and pale surfaces. Avoid large areas of solid colour.

## Rubber-stamp treatment

Render every colour as a separately hand-stamped layer.

Include:

- Authentic carved-rubber texture
    
- Hand-engraved marks
    
- Uneven line widths
    
- Irregular contour notches
    
- Fractured and incomplete edges
    
- Dry ink shortages
    
- Granular ink deposits
    
- Small pinholes and paper show-through
    
- Uneven printing pressure
    
- Faint partial ghosting
    
- Approximately 1–2 mm of natural misregistration between colours
    

Allow slight misalignment between colour layers. Edges must remain rough and analog rather than digitally smoothed.

The result should resemble a real hand-carved stamp pressed onto fibrous paper, not a photograph processed with a filter.

## Mood

Create the feeling of a field note kept by an architect, engineer, travel writer or natural observer.

The image should feel quiet, restrained, tactile, regionally or culturally specific, slightly nostalgic and collectible. It should capture the most recognisable fragments of a memory rather than document everything literally.

## Text

Use **no captions, titles, dates, labels or decorative lettering**.

If a word, marking or brand name is intrinsic to recognising the subject, it may appear **once**, small and imperfectly stamped. Include no slogans, supporting copy or repeated branding.

## Avoid

Avoid full-page illustrations, photographic realism, glossy product photography, commercial advertisements, tourist souvenir templates, monument montages, generic city icons, smooth vector graphics, clean line-art logos, circular seals, Chinese red stamps, postage-stamp perforations, wax seals, sticker treatments, collage layouts, dense detail, decorative clutter, childish craft styles, cartoons, 3D rendering, plastic textures, glossy gradients, oversaturation, borders, captions and watermarks.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-09-27 03:41:24Z)**_

Root cause confirmed: Charpai converts every upload to FLAC before transcription. The current OpenAI API accepts files up to 25 MB and lists MP3/MP4/MPEG/MPGA/M4A/WAV/WebM—not FLAC—so a valid Telugu recording can reach the API as a large unsupported file and produce exactly this 400 error. I’m changing preprocessing to a speech-optimized, mono MP3 and enforcing the 25 MB limit after conversion.

_**User (2026-09-27 21:04:07Z)**_

Are supplements the only way to go? I was hoping that I would instead get a subpage under stories.here.now/<slug>

---

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-09-27 21:04:14Z)**_

Yes—with a here.now workspace, story sites use subdomains:

`<story-slug>.stories.here.now`

here.now does not currently support mounting workspace sites at:

`stories.here.now/<story-slug>`

Path-based mounts are available only on personal vanity domains or connected custom domains, according to the [here.now documentation](https://here.now/docs).

If you want subpages, the best option is to connect a custom domain such as:

`stories.charpai.com/<story-slug>`

Otherwise, we should retain the current `two-kitkats-332u345f.stories.here.now` format.
